Potato___Early_blight.description: Early blight is a prevalent fungal disease caused by Alternaria solani. It primarily attacks older potato foliage first, producing characteristic dark brown to black necrotic spots with distinct concentric rings creating a 'target board' or bullseye appearance.
symptoms: Dark brown to black circular-to-angular spots on older lower leaves.
Concentric rings ('target-board' or bullseye pattern) within lesions.
Chlorotic (yellow) halos developing around spots as fungal toxins spread.
Premature leaf senescence, drying out, and leaf drop leading to defoliation.
In severe cases, dark, sunken, leathery lesions appear on potato stems.
immediate_actions: Remove and safely destroy heavily infected lower foliage (do not compost diseased plant material).
Cease all overhead sprinkler irrigation immediately; water strictly at soil level early in the morning so canopy dries rapidly.
Ensure adequate physical spacing between potato plants to improve air circulation and decrease humidity in the microclimate.
Disinfect pruning shears, boots, and tools with 70% isopropyl alcohol or a 10% household bleach solution between plants.
prevention: Implement a strict 3- to 4-year crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops (avoid planting after tomato, pepper, or eggplant).
Apply clean straw or plastic mulch around the base of vines to create a physical barrier preventing fungal spores from splashing up from the soil during rain.
Maintain balanced plant nutrition with adequate potassium and moderate nitrogen (stressed or senescing plants are much more susceptible).
Source certified disease-free seed tubers and select cultivars with documented tolerance.

fungicides: Preventative protectants: Chlorothalonil or Mancozeb applied before canopy closure and continued at 7- to 10-day intervals depending on disease pressure.
Targeted systemic fungicides: Azoxystrobin, Pyraclostrobin, or Difenoconazole rotated to adhere to FRAC guidelines and prevent resistance.
Organic / Bio-fungicides: Fixed copper fungicides (copper hydroxide/copper sulfate) or Bacillus subtilis (QST 713 strain).
treatments.precautions: Always adhere strictly to manufacturer label instructions, personal protective equipment (PPE) requirements, and local Pre-Harvest Intervals (PHI).

Potato___Early_blight.expert_consultation: Consult a local university extension specialist or certified agronomist if defoliation exceeds 15% before tuber bulking or if high temperatures (24-30°C) coincide with frequent dew periods.
sources: Cornell University Cooperative Extension - Vegetable MD Online
University of California Statewide Integrated Pest Management Program (UC IPM)
Potato___Early_blight.disclaimer: Diagnostic guidance is based on machine vision and agricultural extension literature. Verify locally with certified crop advisors and always comply with official pesticide regulations.

Potato___Late_blight.description: Late blight is a devastating, fast-moving disease caused by the oomycete water mold Phytophthora infestans. Famous historically for causing the Great Irish Famine, it can destroy entire fields of potatoes within a few days under cool, wet weather conditions.
symptoms: Pale green to water-soaked circular lesions that rapidly expand and turn purplish-brown or dark black.
Delicate white cottony/fuzzy fungal growth (sporangiophores) visible on the undersides of leaves and at lesion borders in humid conditions.
Water-soaked dark lesions rapidly girdling potato stems, causing plant collapse.
Infected tubers exhibit irregular, sunken, dry brown-to-purplish rot penetrating into the flesh.
Distinct foul, decaying odor in fields with advanced canopy destruction.
immediate_actions: CRITICAL: Act immediately. Late blight produces billions of airborne sporangia that infect surrounding fields.
Carefully bag and destroy infected plants immediately (bury deeply or incinerate where permitted; never compost).
Completely halt overhead watering and reduce irrigation frequency to lower canopy moisture.
Kill vines (vine desiccation) 2-3 weeks prior to harvest if late blight is present to prevent spore wash-down onto tubers.
prevention: Plant strictly certified disease-free seed potatoes from certified seed growers.
Eliminate all cull piles, volunteer potato plants, and wild solanaceous weeds (such as nightshade) around fields.
Provide wide row spacing (minimum 36 inches) oriented with prevailing winds to accelerate canopy drying.
Hill up soil generously (at least 8-10 cm cover over tubers) to create an effective soil buffer against spore penetration.

fungicides: Preventative protectants: Mancozeb, Chlorothalonil, or Fluazinam applied prior to infection or when local weather alerts (e.g. Blitecast) trigger warnings.
Systemic / Curative oomycides: Cymoxanil, Dimethomorph, Fluopicolide, or Mandipropamid used in alternation according to FRAC anti-resistance management.
Organic management: Fixed copper formulations applied strictly preventatively before infection occurs.
treatments.precautions: Late blight pathogens develop resistance rapidly. Never apply single-site systemic fungicides alone; tank-mix or alternate with protectant fungicides.

Potato___Late_blight.expert_consultation: URGENT: Alert your local agricultural extension service or Department of Agriculture immediately upon suspected detection. Late blight is a community-level quarantine threat.
sources: Cornell University Late Blight Decision Support System
Potato___Late_blight.disclaimer: Late blight is an aggressive, high-consequence plant disease. Adhere to statutory pest notifications in your jurisdiction and verify all management actions with regional crop specialists.

Potato___healthy.description: The inspected foliage shows vibrant, healthy characteristics with uniform chlorophyll pigmentation, intact leaf margins, and no visible necrotic lesions, chlorosis, or pathogen signs.
symptoms: Uniform vibrant green coloration across upper and lower leaf surfaces.
Clean, smooth leaf margins without curling, speckling, or necrotic margins.
Turgid leaf structure and sturdy stems with no water-soaked streaks or fungal fuzz.
Vigorous canopy architecture supporting active photosynthesis.
immediate_actions: Continue regular crop scouting: inspect lower canopy and leaf undersides at least twice weekly.
Ensure steady, regular irrigation matching the current growth stage (e.g., tuber initiation vs bulking).
Protect foliage from physical abrasion during weeding or tractor passes.
prevention: Maintain soil organic matter and balanced N-P-K fertilizer applications based on regular soil testing.
Employ drip or furrow irrigation to keep foliage completely dry.
Clean tractors, cultivators, and hand tools before entering healthy fields from other plots.
Monitor local weather forecasts for extended high humidity and temperature drops that favor disease emergence.

fungicides: No chemical fungicide applications are required for healthy leaves.
In disease-endemic regions, preventative organic protective sprays (e.g. bio-stimulants or mild copper) may be scheduled prior to rainy seasons.
treatments.precautions: Avoid over-applying nitrogen fertilizer, which creates overly lush foliage susceptible to sap-sucking pests and fungi.

Potato___healthy.expert_consultation: Routine agricultural extension updates are recommended to stay informed of regional pest and disease alerts.
sources: Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) Potato Crop Production Guide
UC IPM Potato Cultural Care Guidelines
Potato___healthy.disclaimer: Diagnostic evaluation reflects the visible characteristics of the uploaded specimen. Continue regular field scouting for early detection of potential stress.
